checkpoints: Calling `repo.find({ order: { index: "ASC" } })` materializes every row of the audit table into memory before the loop even starts, so the endpoint pays a full-table scan on every single request regardless of how many rows were already verified in a prior call.

The verification loop always seeds `expectedPrev` with `GENESIS_PREV_HASH` and re-walks the chain from index 0 on every call, making the cost O(n) in both time and CPU — one hash recomputation per row, every time, no matter how many earlier calls already proved the older entries intact.

A health/monitoring probe hitting this same endpoint every few seconds turns an already-expensive full-scan-plus-full-recompute into continuous, unbounded load on the database as the audit log grows toward tens of millions of rows.

Storing a periodic checkpoint — `{ count, entryHash, anchoredAt }` — written by a background job lets verification start from the last confirmed position instead of genesis, bounding both memory and recompute work to only the rows appended since that checkpoint.

The checkpoint must be mirrored somewhere the application's own database role does not also control — an external notary, a second datastore, or a SIEM — otherwise the checkpoint is exactly as forgeable as the hash chain it is meant to protect.

Streaming rows instead of loading them all with `repo.find()` (e.g., a query-builder `.stream()` returning a Node `Readable`) keeps memory flat regardless of table size; this is a separate fix from checkpointing, which bounds the recompute work rather than the memory footprint.

An internally consistent hash chain cannot detect truncation: if the newest rows are deleted after the last checkpoint, the remaining chain still verifies correctly, so an incremental scan over the surviving tail has nothing to compare against and would wrongly report success.

Catching truncation requires comparing the current tail's count and entryHash against a value anchored externally and independently of the primary datastore — an in-place edit changes a hash, but a deletion of the newest rows just makes the chain shorter, and only an external anchor exposes that difference.

Moving from full re-hash to checkpoint-based incremental verification shifts the trust boundary from the per-row hash to the checkpoint and the witness's independence, so a sparser anchoring cadence widens the window in which an attacker could time an edit and a truncation to land undetected before the next anchor runs.
